summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in January 1983. Replaced by RFC 838.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

subtitle: Mid-January 1983 snapshot of TCP service adoption across Internet hosts.

tldr.problem: TCP deployment across Internet hosts continued to evolve rapidly, making timely data about service availability valuable for network operators.
tldr.mechanism: David Smallberg conducted another survey on January 11-12, 1983, testing the same three services (Telnet, FTP, SMTP) against 323 hosts from an updated NIC hostname table.
tldr.outcome: TCP adoption continued climbing: 105 hosts now accepted Telnet, 79 accepted FTP, and 79 accepted SMTP. This marked significant growth over just one week from RFC 836, demonstrating accelerating deployment of TCP services as the Internet expanded.

today: RFC 838 published an updated survey, replacing these mid-January results with data from later in January 1983.

sections.title: The Third TCP Connectivity Survey
sections.content:
RFC 837 is the third survey in David Smallberg's series, conducted on January 11-12, 1983. This edition tested 323 hosts for TCP support of Telnet, FTP, and SMTP, using an updated NIC hostname table dated December 31, 1982.

The tests ran on January 11 from noon PST to 8:45 pm, with a follow-up retry of problematic hosts on January 12 from 8 am to 4:30 pm.
sections.eli5: A week after the last check, the researcher tested the list again with an updated list of computers to check.

sections.title: Survey Methodology
sections.content:
The survey repeats the same methodology as RFCs 835 and 836: hosts are looked up in the NIC hostname table and classified by their claimed TCP capabilities, then tested for actual connectivity to each service. Results are categorized as accepted, refused, unreachable, dead, or no service, with FTP results also noting whether anonymous guest access was allowed.

Results are presented in summary tables showing counts by result type, followed by an alphabetical listing and then a listing in NIC hostname table order.
sections.eli5: Same testing as before: check the claims in the hostname table, try connecting to each service, and record what happens.

sections.title: Rapid Growth of TCP Services
sections.content:
TCP adoption accelerated further: 105 hosts now accepted Telnet (up from 91 in early January), 79 accepted FTP (up from 70), and 79 accepted SMTP (up from 72). In just one week, Telnet acceptance grew by 15 percent, showing the rapid pace of Internet deployment. The survey tested more hosts this time (323 versus 315), partly due to new systems being added to the hostname table.

The data reveals that by mid-January 1983, roughly one-third of hosts in the NIC table could be reached via at least one of these three TCP services, a significant achievement for a protocol only recently standardized.
sections.eli5: Growth continued rapidly: about 15 more computers answered for Telnet in just one week. The Internet was growing and getting more connected.

sections.title: Acceleration Patterns in TCP Deployment
sections.content:
Comparing the three January 1983 surveys reveals the exponential nature of TCP adoption: from January 4-5 to January 11-12, Telnet support grew 15 percent in a single week, while FTP and SMTP each grew by 13 percent. Over the two weeks from RFC 835 (December 28-29) to RFC 837 (January 11-12), Telnet acceptance nearly doubled from 61 to 105 hosts.

The data shows regional clusters: hosts at major research centers and military installations were more likely to have TCP support, while many smaller organizations or external networks remained unreachable or offline. These snapshots capture the early critical period when TCP was transitioning from experimental protocol to infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The growth was super fast: in two weeks, Telnet hosts nearly doubled. You could see which groups of computers had adopted TCP and which hadn't yet.
